deep.reconstruction:
Context (Case III): water flows from a vertical vessel AB (height a, cross-section ff) into a horizontal cylindrical tube BC (length b, cross-section gg) and out through an orifice kk. Euler's friction law in E260 is modelled on solid (Coulomb–Amontons) friction. The wall friction is proportional to the local pressure head, coefficient α, and the head includes a constant l. The previous page uses l = 30 ft, which is roughly the water-barometer height, so l is very probably the atmospheric pressure head.

With the vessel very wide (αa/f negligible, 𝔄 ≈ 1, Af ≈ a) and the orifice tiny (𝔤 ≈ 0), the steady efflux head is v = a𝔅 − (1−𝔅)l, where 𝔅 = e^{−αb/g}.

§85. If αb/g is small, 𝔅 ≈ 1 − αb/g, so v = a(1 − αb/g) − αbl/g. Raise the water level until outflow just begins (v = 0). This gives α = ag/(b(a+l)). Euler calls this 'the most certain way' to measure the fluid-friction coefficient α, preferable to capillary tubes (cf. §82).

§86. He takes α = 1/4000 as known and computes a fountain example: a = 100 ft, f = 1, g = 1/10, b = 100, kk = 1/10000. Then 𝔣 = 0 and 𝔤 = k⁴/g⁴ = 1/10000. Also 𝔄 = e^{−αa/f} = e^{−0.025} = 1 − 1/40 + 1/(2·1600) − … = 0.97531. Next 𝔅 = e^{−0.25} = 0.77880, and A = (1−𝔄)/α = 98.760.

§87. The general Case III formula, v = (A𝔅f − (1−𝔄𝔅)l)/(1 − αB𝔤) with B = (1−𝔅)/α, gives v ≈ 69.70 ft. A vertical jet from an opening in the back of the tube would therefore rise only about 69⅔ ft, about 30 ft short of the 100 ft reservoir head. Air resistance would lower it further.

Purpose: an experimental design for determining α, and a practical estimate of how much friction weakens fountains.
errors: Numerics check: 𝔄 = 0.975310, 𝔅 = 0.778801 and A = 98.7604 are correct. The numerator A𝔅 − (1−𝔄𝔅)·30 = 76.9147 − 7.2128 = 69.7018. Dividing by the denominator 1 − (1−𝔅)𝔤 = 0.999978 gives about 69.703, so Euler's 69.701 is essentially the numerator alone. The discrepancy is negligible.
Euler converts 69.70 ft to '69⅔ ft' (69.667), a loose rounding. The '30 ft deficit' is likewise approximate (100 − 69.7 = 30.3).

Physical issue, not algebraic: because friction is proportional to absolute pressure (including the atmospheric head l), the model predicts a flow threshold. Water would not move at all until a > αbl/(g − αb), a yield-stress-like effect that real water does not show. The proposed 'most certain' measurement of α relies entirely on this artifact.

ideas.what: Determining the friction coefficient α from the critical reservoir height at which efflux through a long horizontal tube begins: α = ag/(b(a+l))
ideas.modern_name: threshold (static-friction / yield) measurement of a friction coefficient
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (within E260); the underlying pressure-proportional fluid friction law is generally judged physically wrong

ideas.what: Numerical estimate of fountain-height loss due to pipe friction (100 ft head gives about 69.7 ft jet)
ideas.modern_name: head loss in pipe flow / jet height reduction
ideas.usually_credited_to: Later quantitative laws by Chézy, Prony, Darcy and Weisbach; Euler's pressure-proportional version is superseded

deep.surprise_reason: The page carries out routine numerical applications of the friction model in E260. That model (friction proportional to pressure including atmospheric head) is known and is discussed in histories of 18th-century hydraulics, e.g. Truesdell's Opera omnia introductions. The flow-threshold prediction is an artifact of the model, not an overlooked result.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially faithful to the image. 'atque altitudo aquae in vaſe AB notetur' and the formula α = ag/(b(a+l)) match the print, where the denominator appears as b(a+l). Fraktur symbols 𝔄, 𝔅, 𝔣, 𝔤 are correctly rendered.
